**Byzantine Palestine** or **Palaestina** refers to the geographic, political, and cultural landscape of Palestine during the period of Byzantine rule (early 4th to mid-7th centuries CE), beginning with the consolidation of Constantine's power in the early 4th century CE and lasting until the Arab-Muslim conquest in the 7th century CE. The term generally designates the territories reorganized into the provinces of _Palaestina Prima, Secunda,_ and _Tertia_ (or _Salutaris_) between the late 4th and 5th centuries (covering most of modern-day Israel and Palestine and parts of Jordan and Syria.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Byzantine_Palestine#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHerr202219-22-1)[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Byzantine_Palestine#cite_note-FOOTNOTEParker1999135-137-2)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Byzantine_Palestine#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChanceyPorter2001165-3)

The title "Byzantine" is a modern and artificial term which has been called "imaginary".[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Byzantine_Palestine#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBar2004311-4) This division is not unique for Palestine and related to the historiographical line between Ancient history and the Middle Ages. The Byzantine period in Palestine was politically a direct continuation of Roman rule, which began with Pompey's conquest in 63 BCE and, from 395 CE, persisted in the form of the Eastern Roman Empire. Culturally, it followed a historical continuum that began in 332 BCE with the conquest of Alexander the Great and the incorporation of the Levant into the Hellenistic world, later evolving into a Hellenistic–Roman–Byzantine sphere. The Byzantine period is most distinguished from earlier times by major religious and demographic changes. Christianity became the state religion and Palestine assumed a central place in the Christian world, while the Jewish, Samaritan and polytheistic populations, facing increasing restrictions, became religious minorities. The Jewish community declined in influence relative to diaspora communities, with the Babylonian Jewish community emerging as the leading center of Judaism.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Byzantine_Palestine#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHerr202232-34-5)
During Diocletian reign (r.284–305 CE) the Empire's political divisions were reorganized. He introduced the Tetrarchy system, where the empire was split between east and west, each ruled by a co-emperor titled _Augustus_. It was later made that each Augustus appointed an heir which would rule half of his domain and bear the title of _Caesar_, making the empire split between four constituent parts. Each of these parts were governed by a Praetorian prefect. The empire was further divided into smaller administrative units called dioceses. While the system of four co-emperors collapsed almost immediately, the provincial division remained intact throughout the Byzantine period. The province of Palaestina was included within the Diocese of the East, part of the Praetorian prefecture of the East.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Byzantine_Palestine#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDi_Segni202279-6)

Since the First Jewish–Roman War (70 CE), the province of Judaea (from the 130s, Syria Palaestina) was administered by governor of a _Legatus Augusti pro praetore_ rank, responsible for military and judicial matters, and a _Procurator_ responsible for financial matters. The capital was Caesarea Maritima and the province included most of modern-day Israel and Palestine, as well as a strip of land called Perea (modern-day Jordan) and excluding the Galilee and Golan Heights regions, which were part of Phoenice, and the Negev which was part of Arabia. The reforms of Diocletian transformed the military responsibility from the governor to a new office: Dux Palaestinae. The governor's role was administering justice, collecting taxes, maintaining the treasury, and preserving public order with a reduced military force. The governor's title changed to _iudex_ ("judge"). His rank was of _praeses,_ later elevated to _consularis_, and in the 380s CE to _proconsul._ This reflects an expansion of his office and the allocation of greater funds.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Byzantine_Palestine#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDi_Segni202279-80-7)

The province of Palaestina underwent numerous transformations during the 4th century CE, the exact chronology of which remains ambiguous. While Diocletian's reforms generally aimed to reduce the size of provinces, Palaestina was enlarged in the south at the expense of Arabia, with the annexation of the Negev, Sinai, and parts of Transjordan south of Wadi al-Hasa around 295 CE. Dora was also annexed from Phoenice. The territories in the south appear to have been transferred between Palaestina and Arabia on several occasions during the 4th century, possibly as many as six times. In some sources, a province called "New Arabia" is mentioned between 315 and the late 4th century, with its capital at Eleutheropolis, though both its boundaries and even its existence are disputed by modern scholars. In 357/8, the southern parts of Palaestina, including the town of Elusa, seem to have been incorporated into a smaller province, which was also called Palaestina (and likely an early predecessor to Palaestina Salutaris) and later reabsorbed back into Palaestina. It is possible that the reunification of Palaestina was linked to the implementation of Theodosius I's religious reforms, and it is around the last years of his reign that Palaestina was divided into three provinces.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Byzantine_Palestine#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDi_Segni202281-90-8)[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Byzantine_Palestine#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAvi-Yonah2002119-125-9)

### Frequently Asked Questions
#### What is meant by the "Byzantine Holy Land"?
It refers to the roughly three centuries, from the early fourth century to the Muslim conquest in the seventh century, when the Holy Land formed part of the Christian Roman Empire and Jerusalem, Bethlehem, Galilee, and the Judean Desert were extensively developed with churches, monasteries, and pilgrim infrastructure.

## Three centuries that turned Jerusalem, Bethlehem, and Galilee into a Christian landscape
### Frequently Asked Questions
#### Who was Empress Eudocia and what did she build in Jerusalem?
Eudocia was a fifth-century Roman empress who eventually settled in Jerusalem. She became one of the city's major Christian patrons, associated with new fortifications, churches including a basilica honoring Saint Stephen, and charitable institutions serving the poor and pilgrims.

## Three centuries that turned Jerusalem, Bethlehem, and Galilee into a Christian landscape
### Frequently Asked Questions
#### What was Justinian's Nea Church?
The Nea Church, consecrated in Jerusalem in 543, was an enormous basilica funded by Emperor Justinian. Procopius described its construction as a major engineering undertaking, and substantial remains of the church were uncovered by twentieth-century archaeologists.

## Three centuries that turned Jerusalem, Bethlehem, and Galilee into a Christian landscape
### Frequently Asked Questions
#### Why did so many monks settle in the Judean Desert?
Beginning in the fourth century, ascetics such as Chariton, Euthymius, and later Sabas were drawn to the desert's isolation as a place for prayer and solitude close to Jerusalem's holy sites. Their communities developed into an extensive monastic landscape that included Mar Saba.

## Three centuries that turned Jerusalem, Bethlehem, and Galilee into a Christian landscape
### Frequently Asked Questions
#### What happened to Jerusalem during the Persian invasion of 614?
Sasanian Persian forces captured Jerusalem in 614, and many Christian buildings were damaged or destroyed. The relic venerated as the True Cross was carried away. Byzantine forces later recovered the relic, which was ceremonially restored to Jerusalem during the reign of Emperor Heraclius.

## Three centuries that turned Jerusalem, Bethlehem, and Galilee into a Christian landscape
### Frequently Asked Questions
#### What happened to Jerusalem's Christians after the Muslim conquest?
Jerusalem negotiated terms of surrender during the Muslim conquest, probably in 638. Christian communities, churches, monasteries, and pilgrimage continued under Muslim rule, although the political framework of the Holy Land had fundamentally changed.

## Three centuries that turned Jerusalem, Bethlehem, and Galilee into a Christian landscape
### Closing Reflection
What strikes anyone who spends time with this period is how much of it survives by accident as much as design. An empress's exile becomes a chapter in Jerusalem's walls. A court historian's boast about ox-teams becomes a rare written witness to a church otherwise reduced to foundation stones. A traveler's reports to distant Christian women become the clearest window historians have into how Jerusalem prayed sixteen centuries ago. A mosaic floor in Jordan preserves a map of a city whose Byzantine streets and monuments would otherwise be far harder to reconstruct.
And then there is Mar Saba. Monks still descend the same desert gorge where Sabas established his community in the fifth century, long after the emperors who ruled the Holy Land disappeared. Bethlehem's great basilica still rises above the traditional place of Christ's birth. Christians still gather at the Holy Sepulchre. Pilgrims still move between Jerusalem, Bethlehem, the Mount of Olives, and Galilee, following a sacred geography that Byzantine Christians helped give physical form.
Empires rise in this story and empires fall — Roman rule becomes Christian Roman rule, Jerusalem falls to Persia and returns to Byzantium, and Byzantine authority finally gives way to Muslim government. Yet the churches, desert cells, pilgrim roads, mosaics, liturgies, and memories outlasted the political world that created them.
That may be the Byzantine Holy Land's most enduring legacy. It did not create Christianity's attachment to Jerusalem, Bethlehem, or Galilee. Those memories reached back to the beginnings of the faith. What the Byzantine centuries did was give those memories architecture, roads, monasteries, processions, mosaics, institutions, and a landscape through which Christians could physically walk.
Much of that landscape is still there.
